plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old needs the root-power meaning made concrete before the number-classification rules, so the lesson moves from a hook, to a rule card and worked anatomy, to guided practice, then to the rational/irrational contrast and its traps, ending with a memory anchor. Each struggle-prone idea (a^(1/2) is not a/2, irrational sums can be rational) gets its own interactive or trap block.
coverage: Rewrite a^(1/n) as the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) as the nth root of a raised to m (or the mth power of the nth root)
Evaluate rational exponents on numbers, including negative bases and fractional results, and connect them to radical notation
Explain why the exponent rules (product, quotient, power) still work for rational exponents
Define rational numbers as ratios of integers with terminating or repeating decimals; irrational numbers as non-repeating, non-terminating decimals
Classify numbers as rational or irrational, including roots like sqrt(4) vs sqrt(2) and familiar constants like pi
State and justify the rules: rational + rational = rational, rational + irrational = irrational, rational x irrational = irrational (nonzero rational), irration
Recognize the common error of assuming every sum or product involving an irrational is irrational, and the error of treating a^(1/2) as a/2
Use rational-exponent and rational/irrational reasoning to simplify and estimate expressions

blocks.purpose: Open with the surprising fact that a^(1/2) is a root, not half, grabbing attention and surfacing the misconception before it hardens.

data.caption: An exponent of 1/2 asks for a square root. It does not cut the number in half.
data.context: Half of 16 is 8, so 16^(1/2) looks like it should be 8. It is not. The fraction 1/2 in the exponent means root, and the square root of 16 is 4. The same idea runs through every rational exponent you will meet today.

blocks.purpose: Give the anchor definition: a^(1/n) = nth root of a and a^(m/n) = nth root of a^m, with the three prerequisite facts (root meaning, power meaning, exponent rules).

data.ruleName: Rational exponents are roots and powers
data.anchor: a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) is the nth root of a raised to the m.
prerequisites: The nth root of a is the number that, raised to the nth power, gives a (for even n, the nonnegative one): the cube root of 8 is 2 because 2^3 = 8.
A positive whole-number exponent means repeated multiplication: a^m is a multiplied by itself m times.
For positive bases, the exponent rules still hold: a^p times a^q = a^(p+q), a^p divided by a^q = a^(p-q), and (a^p)^q = a^(pq).
A negative exponent means reciprocal: a^(-m/n) = 1 divided by a^(m/n), so 4^(-1/2) = 1/2.

blocks.purpose: Break down a worked example like 8^(2/3) and 16^(1/2) part by part so learners see which number is the root and which is the power.

data.title: Anatomy of 8^(2/3)
data.caption: The denominator of the exponent tells you which root to take. The numerator tells you the power.

labels.pickerAria: Choose a part of the expression 8^(2/3)

parts.label: The base, 8
parts.description: The base is the number you take a root of and then raise to a power.

parts.label: The denominator, 3
parts.description: The bottom of the fraction is the root. A 3 means cube root.
parts.example: The cube root of 8 is 2, because 2 times 2 times 2 = 8.

parts.label: The numerator, 2
parts.description: The top of the fraction is the power you raise the root to.

parts.label: The fraction bar
parts.role: Joins root and power, root first
parts.description: The bar joins the root and the power in one exponent. Take the root first to keep the numbers small, then apply the power.
parts.example: 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4. Doing it the other way, 8^2 = 64, and the cube root of 64 is also 4.

blocks.purpose: Contrast rational numbers (ratio of integers, terminating or repeating decimals) with irrational numbers (non-repeating, non-terminating), including sqrt(4) vs sqrt(2) and pi.

data.title: Rational versus irrational numbers
data.subtitle: The decimal tells the story: rational decimals settle down, irrational decimals never do.

items.label: Ratio of integers
items.text: A rational number can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not zero.

items.label: Decimals that settle
items.text: The decimal either terminates or repeats a block forever.

items.label: Roots of perfect squares
items.text: The square root of a perfect square is a whole number, so it is rational.
items.example: sqrt(4) = 2, which is rational.

items.label: Approximations of pi
items.text: Decimals and fractions that approximate pi are rational, even though pi is not.
items.example: 3.14 = 314/100 and 22/7 are both rational.

items.label: Not a ratio of integers
items.text: No fraction of two integers equals an irrational number.
items.example: sqrt(2) cannot be written as a/b.

items.label: Decimals that never settle
items.text: The decimal never ends and never repeats a block.
items.example: sqrt(2) = 1.41421356... keeps going with no pattern.

items.label: Roots of non-perfect squares
items.text: The square root of a positive integer is irrational unless that integer is a perfect square.
items.example: sqrt(2) is irrational; sqrt(9) = 3 is rational.

items.label: Famous constants
items.text: pi is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly.
items.example: pi = 3.14159... never ends or repeats.

data.footnote: A decimal that looks random is not automatically irrational. Check whether it repeats: 0.121212... is rational because it equals 4/33.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the sum and product rules side by side: rational+rational, rational+irrational, rational x irrational, and the either-case for irrational+irrational and irrational x irrational.

data.title: What happens when you add or multiply?
data.subtitle: Rational numbers are closed under addition and multiplication. Irrational numbers are not.

items.label: rational + rational
items.text: Adding two rational numbers gives a rational number.
items.example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, which is rational.

items.label: rational x rational
items.text: Multiplying two rational numbers gives a rational number.
items.example: (2/3) times (9/4) = 3/2, which is rational.

items.label: rational + irrational
items.text: Adding a rational to an irrational always gives an irrational.
items.example: 1 + sqrt(2) is irrational. If it equaled a rational s, then sqrt(2) = s - 1 would be rational, which is false.

items.label: nonzero rational x irrational
items.text: Multiplying an irrational by a nonzero rational always gives an irrational.
items.example: 3 times sqrt(2) is irrational. If it equaled s, then sqrt(2) = s/3 would be rational.

items.label: irrational + irrational
items.text: The sum can be rational or irrational, so you must check.
items.example: sqrt(2) + (-sqrt(2)) = 0 is rational, but sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) is irrational.

items.label: irrational x irrational
items.text: The product can be rational or irrational, so you must check.
items.example: sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2 is rational, but sqrt(2) times sqrt(3) = sqrt(6) is irrational.

items.label: zero times irrational
items.text: Zero is the exception to the product rule.
items.example: 0 times pi = 0, which is rational.

items.label: The trap
items.text: Do not assume every expression with an irrational is irrational.
items.example: sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2 shows the assumption fails.

data.footnote: Rational + irrational is always irrational, and nonzero rational x irrational is always irrational. Two irrationals together need a check.

blocks.purpose: Target the #1 mistake: assuming every sum or product with an irrational is irrational, and that a^(1/2) equals a/2, revealing why intuition fails.

data.question: Which of these expressions is rational?
data.context: Look at each expression carefully. One of them simplifies to a rational number.
data.commonErrorLabel: Assuming every expression with an irrational is irrational

trapReasons.0: Two irrationals can add to a rational, but sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) does not. It stays irrational.
trapReasons.2: A nonzero rational times an irrational is always irrational, so 3 times sqrt(2) is irrational.
trapReasons.3: A rational plus an irrational is always irrational, so 1 + sqrt(2) is irrational.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: It feels like any expression containing an irrational must be irrational. But two irrationals can cancel or combine into a rational. Here sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2, because squaring undoes the square root.
data.correctReasoning: sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2, and 2 is a ratio of integers (2/1), so it is rational. The other three choices stay irrational: sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) is irrational, 3 times sqrt(2) is irrational, and 1 + sqrt(2) is irrational.
data.recoveryTip: Before calling an expression irrational, try to simplify it. If the irrational parts multiply to a perfect square or cancel by addition, the result may be rational.

facts.fact: a^(1/n) means the nth root of a; for example 9^(1/2) = 3 and 8^(1/3) = 2.
a^(m/n) equals (the nth root of a) raised to the m, which also equals the nth root of (a^m).
Example: 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4. Taking the root first keeps numbers small.
A negative exponent means reciprocal: a^(-m/n) = 1 / a^(m/n). Example: 4^(-1/2) = 1/2.
With an even root, a negative base has no real result: (-4)^(1/2) is not a real number. With an odd root it works: (-8)^(1/3) = -2.
Fractional results are fine: 27^(-2/3) = 1/9; 16^(3/4) = 8.

For rational exponents, the product rule a^p · a^q = a^(p+q) still works; e.g. 4^(1/2)·4^(3/2)=4^2=16. The quotient rule a^p / a^q = a^(p−q) and power rule (a^p)^q = a^(pq) also hold (for bases where the roots are real, usually a>0).
Why the rules work: defining a^(1/n) so that (a^(1/n))^n = a^(1/n · n) = a^1 is what makes the power rule keep holding; for example (a^(1/2))^2 = a.
A rational number can be written as a/b with integers a and b, b not zero.

Nonzero rational × irrational is irrational. Proof: if r·x = s, then x = s/r would be rational. Zero times an irrational is 0, which is rational.

data.prompt: Two students look at 3x^2 + 5x - 7. Which reading gets you further?

A factor is a quantity multiplied with others inside a term, so terms are added while factors are multiplied.
A coefficient is the numerical factor of a term that contains a variable, and a constant is a term with no variable whose value never changes.

facts.fact: A term is a number, a variable, or a product of numbers and variables; terms in an expression are separated by addition or subtraction signs.
A factor is a quantity multiplied with others inside a term.
A coefficient is the numerical factor of a term that contains a variable.
A constant is a term with no variable; its value never changes.
A variable is a letter that stands for a number that can change or is unknown.
In 3x + 5, there are two terms: 3x and 5. 3x has factors 3 and x; coefficient 3; 5 is the constant.
Subtraction can be read as adding the opposite, so in 4x - 7 the terms are 4x and -7, and the constant term is -7.
In -x + 2y, the coefficient of x is -1, and in x the coefficient is 1 (it is usually not written).
Terms are added or subtracted; factors are multiplied. In 2(x+3), the whole thing is one term with factors 2 and (x+3).
In 5x(y+1) + 4, there are two terms; the first has factors 5, x, and (y+1).
Like terms have the same variable parts, such as 3x and 7x; constants are also like terms with each other.
A coefficient is a factor, but not every factor is a coefficient; in 3xy the coefficient of xy is 3, while x and y are variable factors.
A constant like 5 is a term, but it is not called a coefficient because it has no variable attached.
Some textbooks say coefficient can mean any factor relative to the rest (e.g., 3 is the coefficient of xy, x is the coefficient of 3y); in Algebra 1 the numerical meaning is standard.
Common Core standard A-SSE.A.1 asks students to interpret expressions by viewing parts such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

misconceptions: Thinking an expression is only a calculation to carry out rather than an object with parts.
Thinking the terms of 4x - 7 are 4x and 7 (the sign belongs to the term: -7).
Confusing terms and factors: in 3x + 5 the 3 is not a term; 3x is.
Thinking 2(x+3) has two terms; it is one term with two factors.
Calling the constant 5 in 3x + 5 a coefficient.
Believing x has no coefficient; it is 1.
Ignoring the negative sign when naming the coefficient of -x or -4y.
Thinking a variable must be x; any letter can be a variable.

plans.approach: A typical learner needs the concrete picture first, so the lesson builds from single half-planes to the overlap, then to corner points and the best vertex, with retrieval and a misconception trap before the summary. Each block does a distinct job: hook, rule, worked flow, practice, trap, anchor.
coverage: Graph a linear inequality in two variables: solid vs dashed boundary line and which side to shade
A system of inequalities is the overlap of two or more half-planes; the solution is the intersection
Feasible region: the shaded overlap that satisfies every constraint at once
Test-point method to decide which side of a boundary to shade
Vertices (corner points) of a feasible region and how to find them by solving pairs of boundary equations
Evaluate an objective value at each vertex and pick the best (max or min)
Translate a real-world constraint problem into inequalities plus non-negativity conditions
Common errors: shading the union instead of the overlap, wrong solid/dashed, forgetting x≥0, y≥0, testing a point on the line

data.anchor: The solution of a system of inequalities is the overlap of the half-planes: a point is a solution only if it makes every inequality in the system true at the same time.
prerequisites: A single linear inequality graphs as a half-plane, bounded by the line from its related equation.
Use a solid boundary for ≤ or ≥, because points on the line are solutions; use a dashed boundary for < or >, because they are not.
To choose a side, test a point that is not on the line, such as (0,0), and shade the side where the inequality comes out true.

choices: Nothing is wrong; every shaded point is a solution.
The solution is only the overlap: the wedge to the left of (2,2) that is shaded by both inequalities.

data.commonErrorLabel: Shading the union instead of the overlap

trapReasons.0: Shading looks like one big picture, so it is tempting to accept all of it. But a point in only one half-plane fails the other inequality.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: Shading each inequality separately makes a large, connected picture, and it feels like the answer. But a system asks for points that satisfy every inequality at once, so only the part shaded twice counts.
data.correctReasoning: Test (0,3): y ≥ x gives 3 ≥ 0, true, and y ≤ -x + 4 gives 3 ≤ 4, true, so (0,3) is in. Test (3,0): y ≥ x gives 0 ≥ 3, false, so (3,0) is out even though it sits in the other half-plane. The points that pass both form a wedge with its corner at (2,2), opening to the left.

data.ruleName: Best Vertex of a Feasible Region
data.headline: A small print shop finds its best profit at a corner, not the middle
data.caseText:
A print shop makes posters and flyers. Each poster earns $4 profit and each flyer earns $2. The shop has 12 hours of press time: a poster takes 2 hours and a flyer takes 1 hour, so 2x + y ≤ 12. Paper limits total output to x + y ≤ 8. Both x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 apply.

The feasible region has four corners: (0,0), (0,8), (4,4), and (6,0). The profit is P = 4x + 2y.

At (0,0), P = 0. At (0,8), P = 16. At (4,4), P = 16 + 8 = 24. At (6,0), P = 24. The best value is $24, reached at both (4,4) and (6,0).

The owner who guesses the middle of the region might pick (3,3) for P = 12 + 6 = 18, which is worse than the best corners, $24. Checking every vertex is what finds the true maximum.

facts.fact: The graph of a linear inequality in two variables is a half-plane bounded by the line from the related equation.
Use a solid boundary line for ≤ or ≥, because points on the line are solutions.
Use a dashed boundary line for < or >, because points on the line are not solutions.
To test a side, pick a point not on the line (like (0,0) if the line misses it), substitute it, and shade that side if the inequality is true, otherwise shade the other side.
A point on the boundary line is a bad test point because it gives no information about which side to shade.
For y > mx + b shade above the line, and for y < mx + b shade below; this shortcut works only when y is isolated with a positive coefficient.
A system of inequalities is two or more inequalities considered together; its solution set is the points that satisfy all of them, the intersection (overlap) of the half-planes.
In a constraint problem, the feasible region is the set of all points satisfying every constraint at once.

Vertices of the feasible region are corner points where boundary lines meet; find each by solving the pair of boundary equations (substitution or elimination) and check it satisfies the other constraints.
The objective function is the quantity to maximize or minimize, such as profit P = ax + by.
For a bounded feasible region, a linear objective function reaches its max and min at vertices, so evaluate it at each vertex and compare.
Real-world quantities like items or hours cannot be negative, so add x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, which limit the region to the first quadrant.
To translate a problem, define variables, write each limit (time, money, space) as an inequality, add non-negativity, then graph.
Whether answers must be whole numbers (e.g., cannot make 2.5 chairs) is a context decision; a vertex with fractional coordinates may not be allowed.

Always shading above the line regardless of the inequality sign, especially after dividing by a negative or when y is not isolated.

facts.fact: An equation is a statement that two expressions are equal; a solution is a value of the variable that makes it true.
Solving an equation is a chain of logical steps, and each step needs a reason such as a property, definition, or given fact.
Addition Property of Equality: if a = b, then a + c = b + c.
Subtraction Property of Equality: if a = b, then a - c = b - c.
Multiplication Property of Equality: if a = b, then ac = bc.
Division Property of Equality: if a = b and c ≠ 0, then a/c = b/c.
Doing the same operation to both sides keeps equality because both sides name the same number, so applying the same operation to that number gives the same result (like a balanced scale).
Multiplying or dividing both sides by 0 is not allowed as a reversible step: division by 0 is undefined, and multiplying by 0 turns any equation into 0 = 0, losing information.
Distributive Property: a(b + c) = ab + ac, and it also applies to subtraction: a(b - c) = ab - ac.
Combining like terms uses the Distributive Property (e.g., 3x + 2x = (3+2)x = 5x); like terms have the same variable part.
The Distributive, Commutative, Associative, Identity and Inverse Properties are properties of real-number arithmetic used to rewrite one side of an equation; properties of equality act on both sides.
Common error: incomplete distribution, e.g., 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4 is wrong; correct is 3x + 12.
Common error: a sign mistake, e.g., -(x - 5) becomes -x - 5 instead of -x + 5; or subtracting 7 from both sides of x + 7 = 2 and getting x = 9.

Dividing both sides by a variable expression (e.g., x) can lose solutions, since the expression might equal 0; for x² = 3x dividing by x loses x = 0. In linear equations at this level, divide only by nonzero numbers.
To verify a solution, substitute it into the original equation (not a later step) and check both sides simplify to the same number.
Checking in the original equation catches errors made in any step; checking a later line could hide an earlier mistake.
Example: 2(x + 3) = 14. Distributive: 2x + 6 = 14. Subtraction Property of Equality: 2x = 8. Division Property of Equality: x = 4. Check: 2(4+3)=14.
Substitution Property of Equality: if a = b, b can replace a in any expression or equation; it is the justification for checking a solution.
Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive Properties of Equality are other properties of equality, alongside the four operation properties.

misconceptions: Thinking you 'move' a term across the equals sign and change its sign, rather than adding or subtracting the same quantity on both sides.
Thinking the Distributive Property is a property of equality; it is an arithmetic property used to rewrite one side.
Applying an operation to only one side.
Distributing a factor to only the first term in parentheses.
Dividing both sides by a variable expression without considering that it could be zero.
Checking the solution in a later step rather than the original equation.
Believing 'justify' means just describing the operation; the reason should name the property.

plans.approach: A typical learner needs a concrete hook, one clean rule card tying percent, mixture, and unit problems to the same equation idea, then guided practice and a trap that targets the two classic mistakes. The level ends with a compact cheat sheet and a memory anchor so the shared equation structure sticks.
coverage: Percent change as an equation: part = percent × whole, and percent change = (new − old)/old
Solving percent equations by isolating the unknown (finding the part, the whole, or the percent)
Mixture problems: amount × concentration = pure substance, and combining two mixtures into one equation
Unit conversion as a proportion or rate equation (e.g., 1 inch = 2.54 cm) with unit cancellation
Setting up an equation from a word problem: define the variable, translate the relationship, then solve
Checking answers for reasonableness (percent over 100%, units matching, mixture totals)
Common error: adding percents or concentrations directly instead of weighting by amounts
Common error: flipping the percent-change base (dividing by new instead of old) or mismatching units

blocks.purpose: Grab attention with a surprising real percent-change fact (e.g., a price that rises 50% then falls 50% does not return to start) to motivate why the equation matters.

data.caption: A store raises a $100 jacket by 50%, then later marks the new price down by 50%. The final price is $75, which is 75% of where it started.
data.context: Two changes of 50% in opposite directions do not cancel. The first 50% is taken of $100, but the second 50% is taken of $150, so the two percents have different bases.

data.anchor: Many percent, mixture, and unit problems rest on one idea: part = rate × whole.

You can multiply and divide fractions and decimals, and you know that multiplying by a fraction equal to 1 does not change a value.

blocks.purpose: Bridge the abstract part = rate × whole rule to everyday objects (a juice mix, a sale tag, a recipe conversion) so the structure feels concrete.

data.rule: In these problems, a rate acts on a whole to produce a part.
data.ruleDetail: Percent problems use a percent rate, mixture problems use a concentration, and unit problems use a conversion factor. The equation keeps the same basic shape.

analogies.everydayScene: You pour 2 liters of 10% juice concentrate and 3 liters of 20% concentrate into one pitcher.
analogies.because: Each bottle contributes its own liters times its own strength, and the pure juice amounts add while the liters add. The final strength is the total pure juice divided by the total liters.

analogies.everydayScene: A $40 backpack has a tag reading 25% off.
analogies.because: The discount is a part of the original $40 whole, and the rate is 0.25. The part is 0.25 × 40 = $10 off.

analogies.everydayScene: A recipe written in cups needs to be followed with a measuring cup marked in milliliters.
analogies.because: 1 US cup ≈ 236.6 mL, so the ratio (236.6 mL / 1 cup) equals 1 and changes the units without changing the amount.

data.title: Set up any of these problems in five moves
data.subtitle: Works for percent, mixture, and unit questions alike.

steps.label: Name the variable
steps.text: Write what you are looking for, with its unit.

steps.label: Write the relationship
steps.text: Translate the sentence into part = rate × whole, or into the matching template.
steps.detail: A percent increase of p% means new = old × (1 + p/100). A decrease means new = old × (1 − p/100).

steps.label: Match the units first
steps.text: Convert anything measured in different units before it enters the equation.
steps.detail: Minutes and hours, or inches and centimeters, cannot sit in the same equation until one is converted.

steps.label: Solve for the unknown
steps.text: Undo the operations in reverse order to isolate the variable.

blocks.purpose: Confront the top misconception: adding two concentrations directly instead of weighting by amounts, and reveal why intuition fails.

data.question: What is the concentration of the combined mixture?

trapReasons.1: Adding 10% and 20% gives 30%, which is higher than either solution, so it can't be right. Concentrations are not amounts, so they can't be added.

facts.fact: Part = percent × whole, with the percent written as a decimal or fraction (25% = 0.25).
To find the percent, divide part by whole; to find the whole, divide part by the decimal percent.
Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old, then multiplied by 100 to give a percent.
A positive percent change is an increase; a negative one is a decrease. The base is always the old (original) value.
A percent increase of p% gives new = old × (1 + p/100); a decrease gives new = old × (1 − p/100).
A percent can exceed 100% (for example, a quantity that triples has increased 200%), but a part of a whole cannot exceed 100% of that whole.
A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return to the start, because the two percents have different bases (result is 96% of the original).
Mixture: amount of solution × concentration (as decimal) = amount of pure substance.
Combining mixtures: pure substance adds and total amounts add, but concentrations do not add or simply average. Equation: a1·c1 + a2·c2 = (a1 + a2)·c_final.
Example: 2 L of 10% plus 3 L of 20% gives 0.2 + 0.6 = 0.8 L pure in 5 L, which is 16% (not 30% or 15%).
The final concentration of a mixture lies between the two starting concentrations, a useful reasonableness check.
1 inch = 2.54 centimeters exactly, by international agreement.
Unit conversion multiplies by a conversion factor equal to 1, such as (2.54 cm / 1 in), arranged so unwanted units cancel.
Example: 10 in × 2.54 cm/in = 25.4 cm; the inch units cancel.
Setting up word problems: define the variable with units, translate the relationship into an equation, solve, then check in the original context.
Mismatched units (e.g., minutes vs. hours) must be converted before using them in one equation.

plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old needs the AND/OR distinction made concrete before notation, so the lesson opens with a real choice, builds the intersection/union idea with a Venn-style contrast, then practices solving and graphing before consolidating with a cheat sheet. Retrieval and trap blocks target the two classic errors: mixing up AND/OR and forgetting the sign flip.
coverage: Compound inequality = two inequalities joined by AND or OR
AND means intersection: solutions must satisfy both parts simultaneously
OR means union: solutions satisfy at least one part
Solve each part separately using inverse operations, then combine
Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign in each part
Graph AND solutions as the overlap of two rays (a bounded segment)
Graph OR solutions as both rays extending outward (unbounded, two directions)
Write AND solutions as a < x < b and in interval notation (a, b)
Write OR solutions with two separate inequalities and union notation using ∪
Recognize no-solution AND (empty set) and all-real OR cases
Common error: treating AND like OR, or forgetting to flip signs on negatives

blocks.purpose: Pose a real ride-height or temperature scenario where a value must satisfy two conditions at once versus either of two conditions, sparking the AND vs OR question.

data.prompt: A theme-park ride has a safety rule: you may ride only if your height is at least 48 inches and at most 78 inches. A second ride says you may ride if you are under 40 inches or over 60 inches. Which rule is the harder one to satisfy?
data.context: Both rules use two numbers, but the little word between them changes everything. One rule asks you to clear two bars at once. The other asks you to clear just one of two bars.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: At least 48 and at most 78
leftChoice.body: You must be tall enough AND not too tall. Both conditions have to hold at the same time, so only the heights in the middle work.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: Under 40 or over 60
rightChoice.body: You need only one condition to hold. A height of 30 inches works, and so does a height of 70 inches, but 50 inches works for neither.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side contrast of AND (intersection, must meet both) versus OR (union, meets at least one), with plain-language anchors.

data.title: AND versus OR: two words, two different solution sets
data.subtitle: A compound inequality is two inequalities joined by and or by or. The joining word decides which numbers count.

items.label: Both parts at once
items.text: A number is a solution only if it makes both inequalities true at the same time.
items.example: x > 2 and x < 5: the number 4 works, but 6 fails the second part.

items.label: Picture the overlap
items.text: Graph each part as a ray, then keep only where the two rays overlap. When the rays point toward each other, the overlap is a segment between two endpoints.
items.example: x > 2 and x < 5 shades only the stretch between 2 and 5.

items.label: Shorthand chain
items.text: When the smaller number sits on the left, you may write the two parts as one chain.
items.example: 2 < x < 5 means x > 2 and x < 5.

items.label: Interval notation
items.text: Write the two endpoints in order inside parentheses, or use brackets for endpoints that are included.

items.label: At least one part
items.text: A number is a solution if it makes either inequality true. It counts even if it makes both true.
items.example: x < -1 or x >= 3: -5 works, 3 works, and 0 works for neither.

items.label: Picture two rays
items.text: Graph each part as a ray and keep everything either ray covers. The arrows point in opposite directions and the middle stays unshaded.
items.example: x < -1 or x >= 3 shades left of -1 and right of 3, with a gap between.

items.label: No chain allowed
items.text: An or solution cannot be squeezed into one chain like a < x < b, because the middle numbers are not solutions.
items.example: Writing 3 <= x < -1 for x < -1 or x >= 3 is wrong.

items.label: Interval notation with union
items.text: Write each piece in interval notation and join them with the union symbol, which looks like a U.
items.example: x < -1 or x >= 3 is (-infinity, -1) U [3, infinity).

data.footnote: Ask yourself one question: must a number pass both tests, or is passing one test enough? Both means and; one is enough means or.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the procedure: solve each part with inverse operations, flip sign on negative multiply/divide, then combine by overlap (AND) or joining (OR).

data.title: How to solve any compound inequality
data.subtitle: Work on each part with inverse operations, then combine the results with the joining word.

steps.label: Split the parts
steps.text: Separate the compound inequality into its two simple inequalities, or keep a three-part inequality lined up as three parts.
steps.detail: x + 3 < 7 and 2x >= 10 becomes two separate problems to solve.

steps.label: Undo addition and subtraction
steps.text: Add or subtract the same number on both sides of each part. Adding or subtracting a negative does not change the direction of the sign.
steps.detail: x - (-4) < 1 becomes x + 4 < 1, then x < -3. The sign stays <.

steps.label: Undo multiplication and division
steps.text: Multiply or divide each part by the same number. If that number is negative, reverse the inequality sign in every part you touched.
steps.detail: -2x > 8 becomes x < -4, because dividing by -2 flips > to <.

steps.label: Combine with the joining word
steps.text: Keep and or or exactly as it was given. For and, the answer is the overlap; for or, the answer is everything either part covers.

facts.fact: A compound inequality is two inequalities joined by the word and or the word or.
An AND compound inequality is true only for values that satisfy both parts at the same time; its solution set is the intersection of the two solution sets.
An OR compound inequality is true for values that satisfy at least one part; its solution set is the union of the two solution sets.
To solve a compound inequality, solve each part separately with inverse operations, then combine the results with and or or.
Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign; do this in each part that needs it.
Adding or subtracting a negative number does not reverse the inequality sign.
The graph of an AND solution is the overlap of two rays, which is a bounded segment between two endpoints (or a single ray if one ray lies inside the other).
The graph of an OR solution with arrows pointing in opposite directions shows two rays extending outward, with the middle left unshaded.
On a number line, an open circle means the endpoint is not included (< or >) and a closed circle means it is included (≤ or ≥).
An AND solution such as x > 2 and x < 5 is written as 2 < x < 5, and in interval notation as (2, 5).
Interval notation uses parentheses for excluded endpoints and square brackets for included endpoints; infinity always gets a parenthesis. Example: −1 ≤ x < 4 is [−1, 4).
An OR solution such as x < −1 or x ≥ 3 is written in interval notation as (−∞, −1) ∪ [3, ∞), where ∪ means union.
An OR solution cannot be written as one combined inequality like a < x < b; it needs two separate inequalities.
An AND with no overlap, such as x < 2 and x > 5, has no solution; the solution set is the empty set, written ∅ or { }.
An OR whose rays cover the whole number line, such as x < 5 or x > 2, has all real numbers as solutions, written (−∞, ∞).
A three-part inequality like −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 is solved by applying each operation to all three parts: subtract 1 to get −4 < 2x ≤ 6, divide by 2 to get −2 < x ≤ 3.
Dividing a three-part inequality by a negative flips both signs and the order: −6 ≤ −3x < 9 becomes 2 ≥ x > −3, which is written −3 < x ≤ 2.

misconceptions: Treating AND like OR (taking everything shaded by either part).
Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Flipping the sign when subtracting a negative or adding.
Writing an OR solution as a single chain like 5 < x < 2, which is not valid.
Using brackets with infinity; infinity always takes a parenthesis.
Mixing up open and closed circles or parentheses and brackets for < versus ≤.
Thinking an AND with no overlap is an error rather than the empty set.
Thinking 'or' means exactly one part is true; in math it includes both being true.
Writing a three-part inequality in the wrong order, such as 5 < x < 2.
